# Segmented sum on RTX A6000 at `453c56e`: fresh offsets and frozen comparison

This record holds two measurements of the private segmented sum on one
NVIDIA RTX A6000 (`sm_86`) at revision `453c56e04393763dc5839f1da64fb5a0d5244a2b`. Each was repeated in five
independent processes. The first times a call that sees a new offsets layout
every time. The second times repeated launches of one frozen layout. They
answer different questions and have different results:

- With a new layout per call, the private planned sum is slower than
  `torch.segment_reduce` in every row at every size, and the best
  configuration of a looped Triton kernel with no planner is at or below
  torch.
- With a frozen layout, the mixed policy is faster than
  `torch.segment_reduce` on eight rows and equal to it on `uniform`. It is
  faster than a looped Triton kernel on the rows of short segments and on
  the one row with segments above 4,096 elements, and slower on the four
  rows that mix short segments with segments of up to 4,096 elements.

These are research measurements, not a performance gate. The machine was not
idle while they were taken; [Machine and conditions](#machine-and-conditions)
says what ran.

The records name revision `453c56e`. The branch history was rewritten after
the runs, to remove a directory that the measurements do not use, so that
commit is not in the published history. Its counterpart is `4e87184`: the
two trees differ only in the removed files, and every file the harness
imports, hashes, or compiles is identical.

## What was measured

### Fresh offsets

`benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py` gives every iteration an offsets
layout that no earlier iteration used. The timed region of every candidate
runs from offsets in to result out. Three sizes were run, each once without
the pad-to-max candidate and once with every candidate. The facts below are
quoted from the records:

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Segments per layout | 2,048, 8,192, and 32,768 |
| Distributions | `uniform`, `log-normal`, `bimodal`, `zipf-like`, `many-tiny`, `few-huge`, `one-outlier`, `alternating-empty`, `power-law` |
| Seed | 7 |
| Layout seeds | seed plus the iteration index, warmups first |
| Layout reuse | none; every iteration takes the next unused layout |
| Warmup layouts per row | 5 |
| Timed layouts per row | 100 |
| Warm step | before each sample, 2 untimed calls of the same candidate on the row's warm layout, each followed by a synchronize; the warm layout has its own seed and its own output buffer and is never timed or checked |
| Values | CPU seeded randint(1, 8) / 4, float32, never zero; one buffer per distribution, each layout reads its prefix |
| Candidate order | a new random permutation every iteration, shuffled by random.Random(order\_seed) with order\_seed '\<seed\>:\<distribution\>:\<iteration\>'; the seed and the order are recorded with each iteration |
| Clock | time.perf\_counter\_ns between two device synchronizations |
| Correctness | every candidate in every iteration, warmups included, against a float64 CPU torch.segment\_reduce reference: exactly where sums of the values are exact in f32 in any order, otherwise within gamma(n - 1) times the sum of magnitudes; each row counts its exact, bounded, and unchecked segments |

The candidates, and what the timed region of each covers:

| Candidate | Timed region |
|---|---|
| `swage_cta_call` | one launch\_gpu call (offset validation and transfer to the host, then one launch of the pure CTA kernel, which walks each segment in 128-thread blocks), then synchronize; no classification and no task upload |
| `swage_mixed` | \_prepare\_planned\_sum (offset validation and transfer to the host, classification, whatever kernel compilation and module loading the preparation path performs at this revision, task upload), then the mixed launch and synchronize |
| `torch` | torch.segment\_reduce on the device offsets with its output allocation, then synchronize |
| `torch_pad_to_max` | pure PyTorch: reading the longest length from the device offsets, padding every segment with zeros to it, the masked row sum, their allocations, then synchronize |
| `triton_looped` | one launch of the looped kernel, then synchronize; it needs no host classification |
| `triton_planned` | the partition (two torch.nonzero calls over the segment lengths on the device, each waiting for the device, and the conversion of the ids to int32), then the packed launch of the short tasks, one launch that reads one block of 4096 elements per longer task, then synchronize |
| `triton_planned_looped` | the partition (two torch.nonzero calls over the segment lengths on the device, each waiting for the device, and the conversion of the ids to int32), then the packed launch of the short tasks, one launch whose longer tasks loop over their segment in fixed blocks, then synchronize |

The Triton candidates are swept: `triton_looped` and `triton_planned_looped`
over 15 block and warp configurations, and `triton_planned` over 4 warp
settings. The record adds this about the Swage candidates:

> swage\_mixed times \_prepare\_planned\_sum with select\_schedule=False. The private runner has no mixed-only preparation: one call returns the warp, CTA, and mixed policies, and only mixed is launched. The two unused policies cost their kernel and module memo lookups and the memoized identity task ids. swage\_cta\_call times the one private call that validates and launches a single policy; it does not classify

The public `swage.segment_reduce` call is not a candidate. `swage_mixed` is
the private preparation with schedule selection disabled, followed by the
mixed launch. The public call prepares and launches the same mixed policy
with automatic schedule selection, and it allocates its result when no `out`
is passed.

### Frozen comparison

`benchmarks/benchmark_triton_comparison.py` prepares one layout per row once
and times repeated launches of it. Preparation, compilation, and the Triton
task lists are outside the timed launch. The three Swage policies come from
`_prepare_planned_sum`, which uses the default limits and disables schedule
selection. The facts below are quoted from the records:

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Segments per row | 32,768 |
| Distributions | `uniform`, `log-normal`, `bimodal`, `zipf-like`, `many-tiny`, `few-huge`, `one-outlier`, `alternating-empty`, `power-law` |
| Seeds | 7 |
| Values | `ones`: every value is one |
| Warmups per candidate | 25 |
| Samples per candidate | 100 |
| Launches per event or graph sample | 32 |
| Batching | event-timed samples batch at least batched\_launches launches; while one event timer tick is not below one percent of the median sample, the batch doubles and the samples are taken again; every timing entry records its launches\_per\_sample, the tick, and the tick as a fraction of the sample |
| Candidate order | each candidate is timed to completion in the order of the row's candidate\_order; candidates are not interleaved |
| Correctness | every timed candidate is checked on the timed values against a float64 CPU reference: exactly where sums of the values are exact in f32 in any order, otherwise within gamma(n - 1) times the sum of magnitudes; each row counts its exact, bounded, and unchecked segments |

The baselines, as the record describes them:

| Candidate | Description |
|---|---|
| `triton (fixed)` | one program per segment, one masked block; blocks smaller than the longest segment are excluded |
| `triton_looped` | one program per segment, a loop over the segment in fixed blocks; no block is excluded for the longest segment |
| `triton_planned` | the task lists come from a device nonzero over the segment lengths, outside the timed launch; short tasks are packed four per program and each longer task reads one block of 4096 elements, so a longer segment skips the baseline |
| `triton_planned_looped` | the same task lists and packed short tasks; each longer task loops over its segment in fixed blocks, with the block and warp sweep of triton\_looped, so no segment length skips it |
| `torch_padded` | pure PyTorch: every segment padded with zeros to the longest one outside the timed launch, then the masked matrix summed per row inside it |

## How the tables are built

- Every process contributes the median of its own samples. A cell in
  microseconds is the median of the five per-process medians.
- A ratio is formed inside each process from its two medians. A ratio cell
  gives the median of the five ratios and, in brackets, their minimum and
  maximum. Ratios to torch are the ones the summaries hold. The other
  ratios are formed by the same rule from the per-process medians in the
  summaries.
- Microseconds are rounded to one decimal and ratios to two.
- A "best" Triton configuration is the one with the lowest median in that
  row. It is chosen after the run from a sweep, separately for every row,
  so it is an optimistic bound for a Triton user who must pick one
  configuration in advance. The tables also count how many configurations
  of the sweep are at or below torch, or faster than the Swage candidate.
- Two medians within 2 percent of each other are called
  equal in the statements.

## Fresh offsets: a new layout on every call

With a new offsets layout on every call, the private planned sum (`swage_mixed`: preparation with schedule selection disabled, then the mixed launch) took longer than `torch.segment_reduce`: 2.69 to 6.07 times as long at 2,048 segments (slower in every process in every one of the 9 rows); 1.73 to 4.44 times as long at 8,192 segments (slower in every process in every one of the 9 rows); 1.31 to 2.85 times as long at 32,768 segments (slower in every process in every one of the 9 rows). Each figure is the median across five processes of the ratio of the two per-process medians, and the range is over the nine distributions.

The single-policy call (`swage_cta_call`), which validates the offsets and launches the pure CTA kernel without classifying, also took longer than `torch.segment_reduce`: 1.96 to 3.46 at 2,048 segments (slower in every process in every one of the 9 rows); 1.38 to 2.76 at 8,192 segments (slower in every process in every one of the 9 rows); 1.15 to 2.91 at 32,768 segments (slower in every process in every one of the 9 rows). The loss is therefore not the planner alone.

A looped Triton kernel with no planner, one program per segment that walks the segment in fixed blocks, is at or below `torch.segment_reduce` in the same regime. Taking the best of its 15 block and warp configurations per row, chosen after the run, its ratio to torch is 0.78 to 0.94 at 2,048 segments (median at or below one in every one of the 9 rows; the largest ratio of any process is 0.94); 0.67 to 0.99 at 8,192 segments (median at or below one in every one of the 9 rows; the largest ratio of any process is 0.99); 0.49 to 0.99 at 32,768 segments (median at or below one in every one of the 9 rows; the largest ratio of any process is 1.05). Not every configuration is: the fewest at or below torch are 14 of 15 on `alternating-empty` at 2,048 segments, 4 of 15 on `power-law` at 8,192 segments, 1 of 15 on `power-law` at 32,768 segments. The tables give the count for each row.

Planned Triton with its partition inside the timed region (two `torch.nonzero` calls over the lengths, then a packed launch) is slower than `torch.segment_reduce` at every size. Taking the best of its configurations per row, chosen after the run: at 2,048 segments it took 3.30 to 6.48 times as long as torch, and `swage_mixed` took 0.79 to 0.93 times as long as it (Swage faster in every one of the 9 rows); at 8,192 segments it took 1.88 to 4.55 times as long as torch, and `swage_mixed` took 0.86 to 1.02 times as long as it (Swage faster in 7 of the 9 rows); at 32,768 segments it took 1.25 to 2.10 times as long as torch, and `swage_mixed` took 1.04 to 1.79 times as long as it (Swage faster in none of the 9 rows).

The range of each ratio over the nine distributions:

| Segments | `swage_mixed` / torch | `swage_cta_call` / torch | Best looped Triton / torch | Best planned Triton / torch | `swage_mixed` / best planned Triton |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2,048 | 2.69 to 6.07 | 1.96 to 3.46 | 0.78 to 0.94 | 3.30 to 6.48 | 0.79 to 0.93 |
| 8,192 | 1.73 to 4.44 | 1.38 to 2.76 | 0.67 to 0.99 | 1.88 to 4.55 | 0.86 to 1.02 |
| 32,768 | 1.31 to 2.85 | 1.15 to 2.91 | 0.49 to 0.99 | 1.25 to 2.10 | 1.04 to 1.79 |

### Pad-to-max

Pad-to-max in pure PyTorch (pad every segment with zeros to the longest one, then sum the masked rows) took 2.67 to 1,834.50 times as long as `torch.segment_reduce` on the rows where it ran. The low end is the rows whose longest segment is 32 elements; one long segment sets the cost of every row. It was not timed on `power-law` at 32,768 segments, where the padded matrix does not fit the free device memory.

Each size was run twice, once without the pad-to-max candidate and once with it. The fresh-offsets tables use the run without it, because that candidate allocates a large buffer on every call. The `swage_mixed` to torch ratios of the two runs differ by at most 2.3 percent in any row.

## Frozen comparison: one layout, repeated launches

Graph-replay timing is the primary method here, as in the older comparison
record: it replays captured launches and leaves host dispatch out. Each
statement uses the median across processes of the per-process ratio, at
32,768 segments with all-one values:

- Against `torch.segment_reduce`, `swage_mixed` is faster on `log-normal`, `bimodal`, `zipf-like`, `many-tiny`, `few-huge`, `one-outlier`, `alternating-empty`, and `power-law` (0.17 to 0.64 times as long); within 2 percent on `uniform` (0.99).
- Against the matched planned Triton scheduler (best of 4 warp settings, chosen after the run), `swage_mixed` is faster on `log-normal` (0.87 times as long); within 2 percent on `uniform`, `bimodal`, `zipf-like`, and `few-huge` (1.00 to 1.01); slower on `many-tiny`, `one-outlier`, and `alternating-empty` (1.07 to 1.15 times as long). The comparator was not timed on `power-law`.
- Against the looped Triton kernel (best of 15 configurations, chosen after the run), `swage_mixed` is faster on `many-tiny`, `one-outlier`, `alternating-empty`, and `power-law` (0.31 to 0.48 times as long); within 2 percent on `uniform` (1.01); slower on `log-normal`, `bimodal`, `zipf-like`, and `few-huge` (1.16 to 1.25 times as long).
- Against the looping planned Triton scheduler (best of 15 configurations, chosen after the run), `swage_mixed` is faster on `power-law` (0.51 times as long); within 2 percent on `uniform`, `bimodal`, `zipf-like`, and `few-huge` (0.99 to 1.00); slower on `log-normal`, `many-tiny`, `one-outlier`, and `alternating-empty` (1.07 to 1.28 times as long).

## What the results support

- The private planned sum pays a host preparation on every new layout. With
  a new layout per call, that makes it slower than `torch.segment_reduce`
  on this machine at every measured size and distribution.
- A looped Triton kernel needs no preparation, and the median of its best
  configuration is at or below torch in that regime.
- With a frozen layout, the mixed policy is faster than torch on eight rows
  and equal to it on `uniform`. Its packing of short segments and its
  splitting of very long ones beat a looped kernel on the rows they apply
  to.
- With a frozen layout, a looped Triton kernel is faster than the mixed
  policy on the four rows that mix short segments with segments of up to
  4,096 elements, and a planned Triton scheduler matches or beats the mixed
  policy on most rows.

## What the results do not support

- A statement about another GPU or architecture. One NVIDIA RTX A6000 (`sm_86`)
  ran everything.
- A statement about other seeds. Every row uses seed 7. The
  fresh-offsets layouts of a row differ by iteration, and the comparison
  has one layout per row.
- A statement about other values in the frozen comparison. Its values are
  all one. Fresh offsets uses seeded quarter multiples.
- A statement about a quiet machine. The desktop session was running, the
  GPU was shared with it, the CPU frequency governor was `powersave`
  throughout, and one process started beside another compute process.
- The cost of the public `swage.segment_reduce` call. It is not a
  candidate. The fresh-offsets candidate is the private preparation with
  selection disabled.
- A ranking of Triton configurations that a user could pick in advance.
  Every "best" is chosen after the run.
- A gate. No threshold was declared before the run.

## Reproduce

With the native build, CUDA-enabled PyTorch, and Triton available, from a
clean worktree, and with `OUT` set to a new directory outside the checkout:

```sh
export PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python:$PWD/build/python_packages"
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/fresh-2048-nopad" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 2048 --exclude-candidates torch_pad_to_max
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/fresh-2048-all" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 2048
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/fresh-8192-nopad" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 8192 --exclude-candidates torch_pad_to_max
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/fresh-8192-all" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 8192
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/fresh-32768-nopad" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 32768 --exclude-candidates torch_pad_to_max
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/fresh-32768-all" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_fresh_offsets.py --segment-count 32768
python benchmarks/benchmark_processes.py --processes 5 --output-dir "$OUT/comparison" \
  -- benchmarks/benchmark_triton_comparison.py --suite segmented-sum --distributions many-tiny uniform log-normal bimodal zipf-like few-huge one-outlier alternating-empty power-law
```

A rerun is a new measurement. Do not write it into `benchmarks/results/`.

To regenerate this page and the documentation fragments from the committed
summaries, and to check them and the digests of the compressed process
records:

```sh
python benchmarks/campaign_tables.py
python benchmarks/campaign_tables.py --check
```
